items.title: Kodak invented the digital camera in 1975
items.claim: Steven Sasson, a Kodak engineer, built the first digital camera prototype in 1975. What happened to it?

options.text: Kodak rushed it to market and dominated the digital camera industry
Kodak management, worried about cannibalising film sales, suppressed the project; the company filed for bankruptcy in 2012 having failed the digital transition
It was stolen by a competitor before it could be developed

items.reveal:
Sasson's prototype was a 3.6 kg device using a CCD sensor and a cassette tape, taking 23 seconds to capture a 0.01 megapixel black-and-white image. He filed a patent in 1978.

Kodak's response, as Sasson later recalled, was 'that's cute, but don't tell anyone about it.' Film and processing had 60-70% gross margins. Kodak did launch digital products from the 1990s but couldn't restructure around a business model with lower margins.

The company filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in January 2012.
items.why: Owning the future technology isn't enough — you have to be willing to destroy your current revenue. Few large organisations can.

items.title: Decline is not the end — vinyl records came back
items.claim: Vinyl record sales collapsed from the mid-1980s as CDs took over. What has happened since the late 2000s?

options.text: Vinyl sales have risen every year from 2007 to 2023, overtaking CDs in US revenue terms in 2022 for the first time since 1987 (RIAA data)

items.reveal:
RIAA US data: vinyl revenue fell to under $20m by 2006. By 2022, vinyl revenue was $1.2bn — overtaking CDs ($483m) for the first time in 35 years. UK Official Charts data shows similar pattern from 2008 onwards.

The textbook PLC implies decline is terminal. Brand repositioning, nostalgia and physical-product premiums in a streaming world reversed that trajectory. Other examples: Polaroid film, Kodak Super 8, mechanical watches.
items.why: The four-stage product life cycle is a framework, not a law of nature. Decline can be reversed by changing what the product means to customers.

items.title: Market research said the Walkman would fail
items.claim: Sony launched the TPS-L2 Walkman in 1979. What did market research suggest beforehand?

options.text: Strong demand from young consumers — supporting the launch
Likely failure: consumers reported they wanted recording capability, not just playback, and disliked the absence of speakers
No research was conducted because Akio Morita had no money for it

items.reveal:
Co-founder Masaru Ibuka wanted a portable player so he could listen to opera on long flights. Akio Morita, despite hostile focus group findings, championed the launch. Sony hedged by initially offering it with two headphone jacks (so you could share) and a 'hotline' button to talk to a companion — both later dropped.

First-month sales in Japan were 30,000 units. By the early 1980s the Walkman was a global phenomenon and 'walkman' became a generic word for portable cassette player.

Clayton Christensen later used the case in 'The Innovator's Dilemma' to argue that existing customer research can't reliably predict demand for genuinely new products.
items.why: Market research has methodological limits. Consumers can tell you what they want among options they already know; they're worse at imagining a category that doesn't exist.
